cap1.abertura.p2: The war ended five years ago. The city still bears its scars, but the trams are running through the streets again, and in the parks the old men are back at their chessboards until dark.
cap1.abertura.p3: In the newspapers and on the radio, chess is serious business. The world champion is one of ours, Mikhail Botvinnik, and he has just been handed a challenger: the young master David Bronstein.
cap1.abertura.p4: You are thirteen. Your grandfather taught you the moves on a wooden board that still sits in your room.
cap1.abertura.p5: You don't know it yet, but this is where a road begins, one that could lead all the way to the throne.
cap1.quarto.livro.texto:
An old book of your grandfather's, its cover long gone, full of Capablanca's games. Grandfather used to say the Cuban played chess the way other people breathe: without any effort at all.

In the margins, his tiny handwriting insists, page after page: "Simplify. Always simplify."
cap1.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
The wooden board where you learned the moves. The white knight has had a chipped ear ever since it fell off the table.

For weeks you have only played against yourself, turning the board around after every move. It is time to find real opponents.
cap1.fechamento.aprovado:
The sun has already set when Mr. Ozols puts the pieces back in their wooden box.

"You are not a beginner anymore," he says, without looking up from the box. "Tomorrow afternoon, wait for me here. I'll take you to a place where boys like you learn properly."
cap1.fechamento.reprovado:
Night falls over the park. The old men pack up their pieces and walk home arguing about the day's games.

Nobody is born knowing. Tomorrow they will be here again — and so will you.
adv.peteris.apresentacao: Eleven years old, pockets full of lost pieces. Plays fast and loves bringing his queen out early.
adv.grisha.apresentacao: A retired railwayman. Smokes a pipe, tells war stories and never turns down a queen trade.
adv.ozols.apresentacao: A watchmaker in his early sixties. The "king of the park": nobody remembers seeing him lose twice in a row.
dlg.peteris.inicio: Hey! Are you new here? I'm Pēteris. Old Ozols says I play too fast, but he's the one who plays too slow. Want a game? I'll take Black, it's my lucky colour.
dlg.peteris.depois_vitoria: Oh no! I was going to mate you next move… Almost. I'll get my revenge tomorrow, you'll see.
dlg.peteris.depois_derrota: See? Bringing the queen out early works! Tell Ozols, he never believes me.
dlg.peteris.depois_empate: A draw? Boring. Nobody wins anything with a draw.
dlg.grisha.inicio: Sit down, lad. Thirty years on the rails at Riga station, and now this is my train: sixty-four squares. I'll take White, if you don't mind. Old men have their habits.
dlg.grisha.guerra: During the war we played with pieces made of dried bread, on a board scratched into the lid of a box. When hunger got bad, a pawn that left the board didn't go back in the box… Well, enough sad stories. Shall we play?
dlg.grisha.depois_vitoria: Hmm. You calculate better than you look. A boy like you shouldn't stay in the park forever.
dlg.grisha.depois_derrota: Don't look so glum. I lost the first game of my life to my little brother, and he never let me forget it.
dlg.grisha.depois_empate: A fair draw. Like two engine drivers on the same track who both brake in time.
dlg.ozols.inicio: Hm. The new boy. I've heard about you. Here in the park I'm the last step, you understand? Whoever beats me can go and look for better opponents. Want to try?
dlg.ozols.depois_vitoria: … Well played. It's been a long time since anyone caught me like that. You need stronger people than this old man.
dlg.ozols.depois_derrota: Don't lose heart. I've been repairing watches for forty years: everything worth anything works with patience. Chess too.
dlg.ozols.depois_empate: A draw with old Ozols. That's not nothing, boy. That's not nothing.
dlg.marta.inicio: Good afternoon! Come to fetch your father's paper? Or are you here for the old chess players? They stay until dark.
dlg.marta.op_melhor: Who's the best in the park?
dlg.marta.novidades: It was in the paper: two of ours, Bronstein and Boleslavsky, tied for first in Budapest and had to play a whole match just to decide who challenges Botvinnik. Bronstein won. Soviet against Soviet for the chance to face another Soviet — imagine that!
dlg.marta.melhor: Mr. Ozols, the watchmaker. They say he once drew with a real master, but nobody saw it. He never denied it, either.
not.n1950_budapeste.titulo: A tie at the top in Budapest
not.n1950_budapeste.texto: The Candidates Tournament in Budapest ended with two Soviet players sharing first place: David Bronstein and Isaac Boleslavsky. One of them will be Mikhail Botvinnik's challenger.
not.n1950_desempate.texto: In the play-off match held in Moscow, David Bronstein beat Isaac Boleslavsky 7½–6½ — after the twelve scheduled games ended 6–6 — and won the right to play Mikhail Botvinnik for the world title.
not.n1950_titulos.texto: For the first time, the International Chess Federation has officially awarded the title of grandmaster, to 27 players. Eleven are Soviets — among them champion Botvinnik, Smyslov, Keres, Bronstein, Boleslavsky and the veteran Levenfish.
not.n1950_mezgailis.texto: Voldemārs Mežgailis has won the 1950 Latvian championship, repeating his title of 1944. The women's champion is Milda Lauberte.
not.n1950_final_urss.titulo: The Soviet championship final begins in Moscow
not.n1950_final_urss.texto: Eighteen masters are contesting the final of the 18th USSR Championship. Keres, Boleslavsky and Smyslov were seeded straight in; the rest came through the quarter-finals and semi-finals, including the one in Tartu, just over the border in Estonia.
dlg.marta.op_garoto: Are there any good boys here in Riga?
dlg.marta.garoto: There's Doctor Tal's son, Misha. He won the Latvian junior championship this year! They say that when he was even smaller he knocked on Botvinnik's door — the champion was on holiday here in Riga — asking for a game. The champion's wife told him he was asleep…
cap2.abertura.p2: Since that afternoon in the park, Mr. Ozols has treated you differently. He decided that somebody had to take care of your chess, and that somebody would not be a watchmaker.
cap2.abertura.p3: In Moscow, the world title match has just ended: twelve all. Bronstein was a point ahead with two games to go, but Botvinnik is still world champion. On the park benches, nobody talks about anything else.
cap2.abertura.p4: This afternoon, Mr. Ozols is taking you to the Pioneers' Palace, in the old Riga Castle. Inside, at the end of a corridor, there is a door with a sign on it: Chess Section.
cap2.quarto.saida: Go to the Palace with Mr. Ozols
cap2.quarto.livro.texto:
The notebook Mr. Ozols gave you the day after the park challenge. On the first page, in his careful hand: "A game you don't write down is lost. A game you write down teaches you twice."

You wrote down the three park games from memory. Some of the moves still make you blush.
cap2.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
For weeks, grandfather's board has not rested. You replayed the Moscow match games as they came out in the magazine, one by one, trying to understand how Bronstein, a point ahead, let the title slip away at the end.

Today it stays at home. Today you will play on a board that isn't yours.
cap2.local.vitrine.cabecalho: The display case in the corridor
cap2.local.vitrine.texto:
Small cups, pennants from junior tournaments, photographs of teams standing in a row, all in white shirts. A typed card reminds visitors that the Palace has occupied the north wing of the castle since 1941 and turns ten this year.

You catch yourself imagining your name in one of those photographs.
cap2.fechamento.aprovado:
Mr. Krūzkops looks at the board for a long time, writes something in his notebook and says only: "Tuesdays and Thursdays, at four. Don't be late."

In the corridor, Misha catches up with you. "He said Tuesdays and Thursdays? Then you're in. He never says more than that."
cap2.fechamento.reprovado: Mr. Krūzkops wipes the board clean with the sleeve of his jacket. "Come back next week, there will be another tournament. A lost tournament teaches you something too. Sometimes it teaches you more."
adv.valdis.apresentacao: Thirteen, always the first to arrive. Plays fast when he is nervous, and he is always nervous.
adv.ilze.apresentacao: Fourteen, the only girl in the group, and the one who makes the fewest mistakes. Writes down her games in flawless handwriting.
adv.boris.apresentacao: Fifteen, the oldest in the group. Loves gambits: gives up a pawn early and spends the game trying to prove it was worth it.
adv.gipslis.apresentacao: Fourteen. He learned chess right here at the Palace only two years ago, and he is already one of the strongest in the group.
dlg.kruzkops.inicio: So you're the boy from the park. Mr. Ozols says you gave him a hard time. In the mornings I teach English; in the afternoons, chess. Our group's internal tournament starts today: five players, everyone plays everyone. It's the quickest way for me to see how you play.
dlg.kruzkops.regras: One game per round, with a clock: two hours each. You play Valdis, Ilze, Boris and Aivars, in that order; in the last round you have a bye. The results go on the board on the wall. Whoever scores two and a half points joins the group.
dlg.kruzkops.ativo: Active chess. Nobody here runs away from a complicated position. A quiet position teaches you little; whoever learns to think in the middle of the fire will play calmly anywhere.
dlg.tal.inicio: Are you the new one? I'm Misha. Do you know how I ended up here? I came for the drama group. Then, in the corridor, I saw a door with a sign saying "Chess Section"… I went in, and I never came out.
dlg.tal.op_porta: Is it true you knocked on Botvinnik's door?
dlg.tal.porta: I did! He was on holiday here in Riga, after winning the title. I wanted to play a game with the world champion. His wife opened the door and said he was asleep, and that he was taking a rest from chess. A rest from chess! To this day I don't understand what that means.
dlg.tal.op_torneio: Are you playing the group tournament?
dlg.tal.torneio: Not this one. I already play in the adult tournaments, and I get beaten by real masters, which teaches you more. But I'll be watching your games. One piece of advice: Boris always gives up a pawn. Sometimes it's worth taking it.
dlg.valdis.inicio: Hi… you're the one from the park, right? I play fast, don't mind me. When I get nervous, my hand moves by itself.
dlg.valdis.depois_vitoria: I knew my hand would move before I thought. I always do that. Good game.
dlg.valdis.depois_derrota: I won? I won! Sorry… it's just that I almost never beat anyone new.
dlg.valdis.depois_empate: A draw. For me, that's almost a win.
dlg.ilze.inicio: Ilze. I write everything down, so there's no point arguing about a move afterwards. Good luck in your round.
dlg.ilze.depois_vitoria: You were better today. But it's all written down: next time, I'll know where you go wrong.
dlg.ilze.depois_derrota: I wrote down your game too. Do you want to see where it turned? You don't have to answer now.
dlg.ilze.depois_empate: A fair draw. I'll study the endgame at home.
dlg.boris.inicio: Boris. Do you play book openings? I don't. Books are for people who are scared. I give up a pawn on move three and see what happens.
dlg.boris.depois_vitoria: The pawn wasn't worth it today. But one day it will be, you'll see.
dlg.boris.depois_derrota: See? The pawn always comes back with interest.
dlg.boris.depois_empate: A draw? Nobody gives up a pawn to make a draw. What a waste.
dlg.gipslis.inicio: Aivars. I only learned chess two years ago, right here. So don't be alarmed if I think a lot: I'm still learning.
dlg.gipslis.depois_vitoria: Good game. I took too long in the middlegame and the clock made me pay. I'll remember that.
dlg.gipslis.depois_derrota: Thanks for the game. You played the opening well; the trouble came later.
dlg.gipslis.depois_empate: A draw. It was a serious game. I liked it.
not.n1951_palacio_10_anos.texto: The Republic's Pioneers' Palace, housed since 1941 in the north wing of the old Riga Castle, celebrates its first decade. The Palace's clubs now cover 44 fields of activity, among them the chess section, with nearly a thousand pupils in all.
not.n1951_match_comeca.titulo: World title match begins in Moscow
not.n1951_match_comeca.texto: Mikhail Botvinnik defends his world championship title against David Bronstein, winner of the Candidates Tournament. The match is over 24 games; if it ends twelve all, the champion keeps the title.
not.n1951_match_fim.texto: The Moscow match has ended twelve all. Bronstein won the 21st and 22nd games and led by a point with two to go; Botvinnik won the 23rd, the 24th was drawn, and the title stays with the champion.
cap1.fechamento.tentar: Come back to the park tomorrow
cap3.abertura.p2: For more than a year you have spent Tuesdays and Thursdays at the Palace. Mr Krūzkops hardly praises anyone, but last month he stopped behind your chair, watched a whole game and said only: "It's time."
cap3.abertura.p3: Time for what, you found out the next day: he had entered you in the semi-final of the Riga championship. A grown-ups' tournament. Engineers, army men, university students, people who have played chess since before you were born.
cap3.abertura.p4: You are fifteen. It is the first time someone will look across the board and see you as an opponent, not as the boy from the Palace.
cap3.quarto.livro.texto:
The notebook Mr Ozols gave you is almost full. The games from the class tournament, the ones from the Palace, the ones you played against Misha in the breaks and lost nearly every time.

On the last blank page you wrote the name of tomorrow's tournament, and under it, in small letters, a question: "Will they let me really play?"
cap3.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
The knight with the chipped ear is still in its place. Mr Krūzkops warned you: in grown-up tournaments, a game that isn't finished in the session is adjourned. The move goes into an envelope, and the analysis goes on at home, at night.

If that happens, this is the board where you'll spend the night.
cap3.local.aviso.texto:
Typed, with a crooked stamp at the foot of the page:

1. Two and a half hours for each player for the first forty moves.
2. After the fortieth move the session ends. The player whose turn it is writes down his move and hands it to the arbiter in a sealed envelope.
3. An adjourned game is resumed the next morning, with one more hour for each player.
4. Talking near the tables and analysing in the hall are forbidden.

Someone has added in pencil underneath: "and smoking only in the corridor". Nobody obeys.
cap3.local.jornal.cabecalho: A newspaper left on a chair
cap3.fechamento.aprovado:
The arbiter writes the last result on the table and draws a line under your name. Someone behind you says, quietly: "the boy from the Palace". It doesn't sound like a joke any more.

On the way out, Mr Krūzkops shakes your hand, the way you shake a grown man's hand. "Next year, the final of the Latvian championship. Misha will be there too. Get ready."
cap3.fechamento.reprovado:
The arbiter rubs out your last result and chalks it in again, harder, as if he had to be sure.

Mr Ozols is waiting at the door, hat in hand. "Grown-ups blunder just like children, they only take longer. You saw it. At the next semi-final, they'll be the ones afraid of the boy."
adv.kalnins.apresentacao: An engineer at a radio factory, in his early thirties. He plays the way he builds a circuit: slowly, part by part, never skipping a step.
adv.sokolov.apresentacao: A reserve officer of fifty, always in his tunic. He attacks the king as if taking a hill, and he doesn't like to retreat.
adv.zenta.apresentacao: Twenty, a mathematics student at the university. She works out variations on café napkins and almost never gets into time trouble.
adv.zilber.apresentacao: Nineteen, born in Riga, the strongest in the group. This year he beat Misha Tal. He plays fast, smiles little and forgives nothing.
dlg.ozols_clube.inicio: I closed the shop early today. The park boy's first grown-up tournament: an old man doesn't miss that. I'll be over in the corner, quiet. I promise not to give advice.
dlg.ozols_clube.nervoso: Of course you are. So would I be. A watchmaker's advice: look at the clock only after you've moved, never before. Whoever plays looking at the clock plays in a hurry, and hurry is the one thing I've never managed to fix in anyone.
dlg.ozols_clube.op_adultos: What are grown-ups like at the board?
dlg.ozols_clube.adultos: Just like you, boy. Only they get tired. By the fifth hour the engineer forgets his factory, the major forgets the war, and everybody blunders. Whoever is still in one piece at the end of the session wins. And you are fifteen.
dlg.tal_clube.inicio: You're here! Krūzkops told me. I'm in the other group of this semi-final, so today I only came to watch. Well, to watch and suffer: Zilber ended up in your group. He beat me this year, did you know?
dlg.tal_clube.op_adiada: Have you ever had a game adjourned?
dlg.tal_clube.adiada: Once, in a Palace tournament, when I was still small. The game was adjourned and I thought the position was lost, I almost resigned. That night I dreamt of an idea. In the morning, at the resumption, it took me ten minutes to find the real move, and I won. Ever since, when one of my games is adjourned, I go to bed early.
dlg.tal_clube.letonia: Seventh place. I lost the first game to an opening trap, imagine, me, in a trap. And Zilber beat me. But I beat Pasman, who was the champion. Next year will be different. Next year you'll be there too.
dlg.arbitro.inicio: You're Krūzkops's boy? Welcome. Here the rules are the same for everyone, fifteen or fifty. If you have a question, ask it now: during the game, I don't talk.
dlg.arbitro.op_envelope: How does the sealed move work?
dlg.arbitro.envelope: After the fortieth move, the session ends. Whoever has the move doesn't play it on the board: he writes it on a slip of paper, shows nobody, and hands it to me. I seal the envelope, you both sign across the flap, and it sleeps in my drawer. In the morning I open it, make the move, and the clock starts again.
dlg.arbitro.op_tempo: How much time does each player have?
dlg.arbitro.tempo: Two and a half hours for the first forty moves. At the resumption, one more hour. If your flag falls before that, the game is lost, and there's no point complaining: the clocks are checked every day.
dlg.kalnins.inicio: Kalniņš, pleased to meet you. Engineer. Don't be alarmed by how calm I am: I spend my days building radios, and a radio built in a hurry doesn't play. Chess is the same.
dlg.kalnins.depois_vitoria: Hm. You soldered everything in the right place. Well done, young man.
dlg.kalnins.depois_derrota: Don't take it hard. At the factory we say: every apprentice's first radio crackles. The second one plays.
dlg.kalnins.depois_empate: A draw. A balanced circuit. I liked it.
dlg.sokolov.inicio: Major Sokolov, reserve. So you're the boy. Very well: at the board there's no age, only position. Don't expect me to go easy.
dlg.sokolov.op_guerra: Where did you learn to play?
dlg.sokolov.guerra: In a field hospital, in 1943, with my leg in plaster and a cardboard board. The doctor played better than he operated, thank God for me. I walked out of there playing. Shall we play our round?
dlg.sokolov.depois_vitoria: I retreated too late. I always retreat too late. Well played, soldier.
dlg.sokolov.depois_derrota: That's how attacking is: whoever hesitates loses. You hesitated. Next time, don't.
dlg.zenta.inicio: Zenta. Mathematics, third year. You must be wondering what a girl is doing here. The same thing as you: playing.
dlg.zenta.matematica: It helps you count. It doesn't help you choose. I can calculate a variation to the end; the trouble is that after three good variations I still have to play just one. No professor teaches that.
dlg.zenta.depois_vitoria: You chose better than I did. I'll think about it on the way home.
dlg.zenta.depois_derrota: I calculated it to the end. Sorry, it was a closed sum.
dlg.zenta.depois_empate: A draw. Equality is a beautiful result, you know. In mathematics, at least.
dlg.zilber.inicio: Zilber. I've heard of you, the other one from the Palace. Good. I beat Misha this year; let's see if his friend plays any better.
dlg.zilber.misha: He wanted to complicate things, so I let him. Whoever complicates too much sometimes gets tangled up on his own. Will it be different with you? Show me.
dlg.zilber.depois_vitoria: … Well played. I don't like losing, but I know when the other man played better. See you in the final.
dlg.zilber.depois_derrota: You're good. But you need about a hundred more games like this one.
dlg.zilber.depois_empate: A draw. Against me, this year, that's no small thing. Ask Misha.
not.n1952_helsinque.titulo: On its debut, the USSR wins the Olympiad
not.n1952_helsinque.texto: At the first chess Olympiad it has ever entered, in Helsinki, the Soviet team took the gold: 21 points, ahead of Argentina (19½) and Yugoslavia (19), among 25 countries. Keres, Smyslov, Bronstein, Geller, Boleslavsky and Kotov played. Smyslov and Bronstein won prizes for their boards.
not.n1952_interzonal.titulo: Kotov wins the Interzonal without losing a game
not.n1952_interzonal.texto: The Interzonal tournament has ended in Sweden, near Stockholm: Alexander Kotov won with 16½ points out of 21, without a single defeat. Taimanov and Petrosian shared second place with 13½, and Geller was fourth. The leaders go on to the Candidates tournament, which decides Botvinnik's next challenger.
not.n1952_letonia.texto: The Latvian championship ended in Riga in March: the title went to Jānis Kļaviņš. Among the finalists were the masters Koblencs and Solmanis, last year's champion Pasman, and two young players from the Pioneers' Palace: Israel Zilber, in fourth place, and fifteen-year-old Mikhail Tal, seventh. In the women's event, Milda Lauberte won again.
not.n1952_semifinal_riga.titulo: Riga hosts a semi-final of the Soviet championship
not.n1952_semifinal_riga.texto: Eighteen masters played one of the semi-finals of the USSR championship in Riga in May and June. Ilya Kan won with 12½ points; Tolush, second, did not lose a single game. The home players struggled against the visiting masters: Kļaviņš scored 7½, Koblencs 7 and Pasman 5.
not.n1952_jogos_helsinque.texto: For the first time the Soviet Union went to the Olympic Games, in Helsinki, and came home with 71 medals, 22 of them gold, second only to the United States. In basketball the Soviet team took silver; one of its players was eighteen-year-old Maigonis Valdmanis, born here in Riga.
adv.zilber53.apresentacao: Nineteen, fourth last year. He beat Misha in 1952 and makes no secret of having enjoyed it.
adv.gipslis53.apresentacao: Sixteen, learned at the Palace, like you. He thinks a lot, errs little, and almost never loses the thread.
adv.klavins.apresentacao: Last year's champion of Latvia. He studies physics and mathematics at the university and plays the way he solves an equation.
adv.koblencs.apresentacao: Master of sport since 1945, four times champion of Latvia. The only master in the tournament, and everyone knows it.
adv.tal53.apresentacao: Sixteen, the only university freshman in the tournament. The same old Misha: he complicates everything, and enjoys it.
adv.finalista.apresentacao: One of the finalists of the Latvian championship.
not.n1952_campeonato_urss.titulo: Botvinnik and Taimanov share first place
not.n1952_campeonato_urss.texto: The USSR championship ended in Moscow at the end of December: world champion Mikhail Botvinnik and Mark Taimanov scored 13½ points each. Geller was third and young Viktor Korchnoi sixth. The title will be decided in a play-off match between the two leaders.
not.n1953_desempate.texto: In Moscow, Botvinnik beat Taimanov in the play-off match by 3½ to 2½ and is once again champion of the USSR.
not.n1953_luto.texto: On the morning of 6 March the radio announced the death of Joseph Stalin, the previous night, in Moscow. The country is in official mourning; the funeral will be on the 9th, with a minute of silence across the whole country at noon, Moscow time.
cap4.abertura.p2: After the semi-final came more rounds of qualifying, and you came through them all. Now your name is on a typed list of twenty: the final of the Latvian championship.
cap4.abertura.p3: One master, Koblencs. Ten or so candidate masters. Last year's champion, Kļaviņš. Zilber, Gipslis. And Misha, sixteen, sitting in the same room as you.
cap4.abertura.p4: Nineteen rounds in one month. You will play them all, but not all of them decide anything: most will go by in the background, on the table on the wall. The games that really count, you play here.
cap4.quarto.revista.texto:
This month's issue has the games of the USSR championship, annotated by the masters themselves. You have played through all of them on grandfather's board, one a night.

In the margin of one of them you wrote in pencil: "They make mistakes too. They just make them later."
cap4.quarto.livro.texto: The old notebook ran out at the semi-final. This one is new, hardbound, a present from Mr Ozols, who wrote on the first page in his usual careful hand: "Nineteen games. Write them all down, even the ones that hurt."
cap4.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
It survived the night of the adjourned game, and it will survive a few more. The knight with the chipped ear stands guard on g1, as always.

A month of championship. You will come back to this room many nights with a position in your head.
cap4.local.aviso.texto:
The same regulations as last year, on a new sheet, with a new stamp:

1. Two and a half hours for each player for the first forty moves.
2. After the fortieth move the session ends, and whoever has the move writes down the sealed move.
3. An adjourned game is resumed the next morning, with one more hour for each player.
4. Nineteen rounds, all against all. Ties for first place will be decided by the championship committee.
cap4.evento.luto.texto:
In the morning, the radio in the corridor announces the death of Stalin, the night before, in Moscow. Nobody talks in the hall; the pieces stay in their box until the round begins.

On the 9th, the day of the funeral, the whole country stops for a minute at noon. After the mourning, the championship goes on.
cap4.fechamento.aprovado:
The arbiter writes in the last result and pins the final table to the wall, where it will stay for a week. For the first time, your name isn't at the bottom of anyone's table.

Mr Krūzkops is waiting in the corridor. "You did what I asked, in a Latvian final. Now everyone in that room knows your name. And Misha is already going around saying the next step is the master title."
cap4.fechamento.campeao:
The arbiter writes in the last result, checks it twice, and writes your name at the top of the table in big letters.

Champion of Latvia 1953. The newspapers will spell your name wrong, then correct it. Misha is the first to hug you in the corridor: "It was you, this time. Next year I take it back." For the first time, the history that was already written is not the same any more.
cap4.fechamento.reprovado:
The arbiter pins the final table to the wall. Your name ended up lower than you wanted, among people who have played for thirty years.

"Nobody wins a Latvian final the first time," says Mr Krūzkops. "But you learn. Next year, again."
dlg.kruzkops_1953.inicio: I came to see my pupil in a Latvian final. Seven years teaching at the Palace, English in the mornings and chess in the afternoons, and look at this room: Pasman, Kļaviņš, Klovāns, Gipslis, all of them came through my class. Now you too.
dlg.kruzkops_1953.campo: Koblencs is the only master in the tournament, and he plays like a master. Kļaviņš is last year's champion. Zilber, Pasman, Solmanis, Klovāns: any of them can beat any of them. And Misha… Misha is Misha.
dlg.kruzkops_1953.op_meta: How many points do I need?
dlg.kruzkops_1953.meta: Nine out of nineteen. Whoever does that in a final like this is taken seriously by everyone in this room, Koblencs included. Less is no disgrace either, but I didn't bring you this far for you to settle for no disgrace.
dlg.tal_1953.inicio: You made it too! I knew it. Nineteen rounds, a whole month: it'll be the most fun of the year. And we meet in the last round, have you seen the table?
dlg.tal_1953.calouro: Philology, first year. I'm the only freshman in the championship. You know what they say? That every year the Latvian final is won by a university freshman: Pasman in '51, Kļaviņš last year. Tradition is tradition, and I have great respect for tradition.
dlg.tal_1953.zilber: This year I'll get him. I even know which opening. But I'm not telling, not even you: you play him too.
dlg.tal_1953.depois_vitoria: … You beat me. In the last round, in front of everybody. You know what's funny? I'm not angry. I'm jealous of the game you played.
dlg.tal_1953.depois_derrota: Sorry, I had to complicate things. You know I always have to complicate things. But what a game, eh?
dlg.tal_1953.depois_empate: A draw! Neither of us wanted to give way. In a few years they'll be telling stories about this game, you'll see.
dlg.zilber53.inicio: The Palace boy, in a final. You came up fast. I beat Misha last year; I want to see if this year I beat the two of you.
dlg.zilber53.depois_vitoria: Hm. Twice now I've lost to people from the Palace. It's becoming a habit, and I don't like habits.
dlg.zilber53.depois_derrota: Good game. But I'm still one step ahead. For now.
dlg.zilber53.depois_empate: A draw. Fair. Neither of us saw anything the other hadn't.
dlg.gipslis53.inicio: Both of Krūzkops's pupils in the same final. I bet he didn't sleep last night. Shall we play a serious game?
dlg.gipslis53.op_keres: Is it true you beat Keres?
dlg.gipslis53.keres: In a clock simul, here in Riga, ten boards. He lost two: one to me, one to Misha. Misha was happier about the opening than about the win. I was happy about the win itself.
dlg.gipslis53.depois_vitoria: You played better. I'll take this game home and look at it again, calmly.
dlg.gipslis53.depois_derrota: Thanks for the game. You had chances in the middlegame; I'll show you where later.
dlg.gipslis53.depois_empate: A draw. A serious game, like I said. I liked it.
dlg.klavins.inicio: Kļaviņš. I'm defending the title this year, which means everyone plays me twice as hard. You too, I imagine.
dlg.klavins.campeao: It means playing every game as if it were the last. Last year I was just a physics student who played chess. Now I'm the champion who studies physics. The physics hasn't changed; the chess got harder.
dlg.klavins.depois_vitoria: You played precisely. In physics we say: the result doesn't lie. Congratulations.
dlg.klavins.depois_derrota: Don't be sad. I lost plenty like this before I won my first final.
dlg.klavins.depois_empate: A draw. A balance of forces. I accept it gladly.
dlg.koblencs.inicio: Koblencs. You're Krūzkops's boy. I've heard good things. Here in the final nobody will give you anything for free, not even me. Especially not me.
dlg.koblencs.relogio: Respect the clock. It's the only opponent that never makes a mistake. I've played for twenty years and I still get into time trouble; don't do as I do.
dlg.koblencs.depois_vitoria: … Well played, young man. I didn't expect it. I'll remember your name.
dlg.koblencs.depois_derrota: Don't lose heart. Losing to a master in a final is the best lesson there is, and it's free.
dlg.koblencs.depois_empate: A draw with the only master in the tournament. You can tell Krūzkops.
cap5.abertura.p2: After the Latvian final, a letter came from Moscow. The All-Union Qualification Commission doesn't give away the master title: whoever knocks at the door must pass an examiner. Yours is a master from Vilnius, and the exam is a match.
cap5.abertura.p3: Misha got the same letter. His examiner is Vladimir Saigin, champion of Belarus, a master since 1943. Both matches will be played the same summer, here in Riga.
cap5.abertura.p4: Fourteen games, one a day. You play the ones that decide; the others go by on the board on the wall. Win the match, and the rest is up to the commission.
cap5.quarto.livro.texto: The hardbound notebook is half full. On the last written page, the final Latvian table with your name in pencil, and under it a sentence of Mr Krūzkops that you copied down in the corridor: "A master isn't someone who beats everybody. It's someone nobody can beat easily any more."
cap5.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
The knight with the chipped ear has seen two adjourned games and a whole final. Tonight it sees the beginning of a match.

Fourteen games against the same man. You set up the starting position and sit looking at it, as if it could tell you something about him.
cap5.local.quadro.cabecalho: Qualifying match for the master title
cap5.local.aviso.texto:
A single typed sheet:

Qualifying match. Fourteen games, one a day. Two and a half hours for the first forty moves; after the fortieth, a sealed move and resumption the next morning, with one more hour.

The result will be reported to the All-Union Qualification Commission.

Nobody wrote down how many points are enough.
cap5.fechamento.aprovado:
The arbiter writes the last result on the board and signs underneath. The master from Vilnius shakes your hand, takes a moment to let go, and says only: "I'll write well of you."

Winning is not the title: the commission in Moscow decides, and it is in no hurry. The news comes in September, in a short notice in Sovetsky Sport, with the list of new masters of sport. Misha's name is there. And, not far from it, yours.
cap5.fechamento.reprovado:
The arbiter writes the last result on the board. The master from Vilnius puts the pieces away slowly, like someone in no hurry to leave.

"You'll get another match," says Mr Krūzkops. "The commission doesn't forget who came close. Next time, come closer."
adv.kalvaitis.apresentacao: Master of sport from Vilnius, in his early forties. He came by train just to examine you. He says little, plays slowly and writes everything in a little black notebook.
dlg.ozols_1954.inicio: The watchmaker again, in the corner. Now you have a real examiner, boy, a master who came by train from Vilnius. Me? I only came to see if your clock keeps good time.
dlg.ozols_1954.op_match: Is a match different from a tournament?
dlg.ozols_1954.match: In a tournament you fix a mistake against the next opponent. In a match, the next opponent is the same man, and he remembers your mistake. Fourteen days looking at the same face: whoever loses patience first loses the match.
dlg.kruzkops_1954.inicio: Two of my pupils in master matches in the same summer. If anyone had told me that back in the park days, I wouldn't have believed it. Concentrate: the examiner came a long way to see whether you are a master, not to hand you the title.
dlg.kruzkops_1954.op_regra: How many points do I need?
dlg.kruzkops_1954.regra: Nobody wrote it down. The regulations say the result goes to the commission, and that's all. What I know is that whoever loses the match doesn't become a master. So win the match. The rest is up to them.
dlg.kruzkops_1954.op_comissao: Why does Misha need a match too?
dlg.kruzkops_1954.comissao: In the team championship in Leningrad, he and Kļaviņš both made the norm. The commission thought it too much to give the title to two from the same team at once: Kļaviņš got the title, and Misha the right to a match. He wasn't offended: he's so confident he thinks he'll win.
dlg.tal_1954.inicio: The two examinees of the summer! Mine is Saigin, champion of Belarus. A serious, polite gentleman who doesn't laugh at my jokes. I'll have to convince him at the board.
dlg.tal_1954.saigin: One game a day. I lost one very early, out of pure laziness in the opening, and won the next. Now it's draw, draw, draw… Saigin is a wall. But walls have doors too, you just have to find them.
dlg.tal_1954.gambito: The Belgrade Gambit! Knight to c3, knight to d5, and the world catches fire. I rehearsed it with the Palace crowd, we spent weeks on the craziest lines. Against a serious master, with White, at seventeen: if not now, when?
dlg.kalvaitis.inicio: Kalvaitis. I came from Vilnius to examine you, and I'll examine you carefully. Don't take it personally: it's my job. Today's game?
dlg.kalvaitis.vilnius: A few. Most of them play the opening well and get lost in the middlegame, because they want to impress. A master doesn't impress: a master doesn't lose. If you understand that in these fourteen days, the trip was worth it.
dlg.kalvaitis.depois_vitoria: Hm. Noted. You didn't try to impress anyone today, and that's why you won. Until tomorrow.
dlg.kalvaitis.depois_derrota: Today was mine. But it's a match: there's another tomorrow, and I won't play any better just because I won. Sleep well.
dlg.kalvaitis.depois_empate: A draw. Correct. Correct is also a grade, in my notebook.
not.n1954_kiev.titulo: Averbakh is champion of the USSR
not.n1954_kiev.texto: The USSR championship ended in Kiev in February: Yuri Averbakh won with 14½ points, ahead of Taimanov and young Korchnoi on 13 each. Petrosian shared fourth place.
not.n1954_letonia.texto: Jānis Klovāns, eighteen, who only started playing at fourteen, won the Latvian championship with 15½ points. Mikhail Tal and Aivars Gipslis shared second place.
not.n1954_botvinnik_smyslov.texto: The world title match has ended in Moscow: Botvinnik and Smyslov drew 12–12 after 24 games, and the champion keeps his title. Smyslov won the 23rd game and drew the last, but a tied match favours the man who already wears the crown.
not.n1954_nova_york.titulo: Victory in New York: USSR 20, USA 12
not.n1954_nova_york.texto: At the Hotel Roosevelt in New York, before a packed hall, the Soviet team beat the American team 20–12 over four rounds on eight boards. Smyslov, Bronstein, Keres, Averbakh, Geller, Kotov, Petrosian and Taimanov played; for the United States, Reshevsky on top board.
adv.spassky57.apresentacao: From Leningrad, he turns twenty at the end of January, in the middle of the final, like you. In Amsterdam he was the only one to beat Smyslov.
adv.petrosian57.apresentacao: Twenty-seven, from Moscow, born in Tbilisi. He sees danger before anyone else and almost never loses.
adv.keres57.apresentacao: The great Estonian, forty-one, the neighbour from the north. Second in the Candidates, the idol of half of Riga.
adv.tal57.apresentacao: Misha, twenty, champion of Latvia in 1953, the same child as ever with the same fire at the board.
adv.bronstein57.apresentacao: Thirty-two. In 1951 he drew the title match with Botvinnik. Nobody thinks along such strange paths.
adv.finalista_urss.apresentacao: One of the finalists of the USSR championship.
cap6.abertura.p2: In Tbilisi, in December, Misha got through the semi-final his own way: one win in the first twelve rounds, then six points out of seven. You got through yours, with the last of the six places, too out of breath to celebrate.
cap6.abertura.p3: Now it's the final of the USSR championship. Twenty-two players, twenty-one rounds, a real stage, with wall boards and a full house every night. Keres, Bronstein, Spassky, Petrosian, Taimanov, Korchnoi. You have read about them all your life.
cap6.abertura.p4: Nobody bets on the boy from Riga. Hardly anyone bets on the other boy from Riga either.
cap6.quarto.livro.texto: A new notebook, the third. On the first page you copied out the list of the twenty-two finalists, and sat looking for a while at your own name among them, as if it had been written by mistake.
cap6.quarto.tabuleiro.texto: Grandfather's board stays in Riga this time. The knight with the chipped ear goes in the suitcase, wrapped in a handkerchief, because Mr Ozols said it brings luck and you didn't dare argue.
cap6.local.mural.texto:
One wall board for each game of the round. A young man in an apron moves the pieces at every move with a long pole, and the audience murmurs along.

They say that outside, in the street, there's another wall board for those who couldn't get a ticket, and that some people spend the whole evening in the cold watching the positions.
cap6.fechamento.aprovado:
The last round ends late, with the hall on its feet. Half a dozen journalists copy the final table by hand at the same time.

Half the points or more in a USSR final. In Riga, they say, the federation's telephone never stopped ringing. From today on, whenever someone makes a list of the best in the country, they'll have to write your name on it.
cap6.fechamento.campeao:
The last round ends late, with the hall on its feet, and your name is at the top of the table. Champion of the USSR, ahead of Keres and Bronstein.

Misha crosses the stage and hugs you before anyone else. "You again! Soon I'll have to ask for your autograph." Outside, in the cold, the crowd at the street board still hasn't gone home.
cap6.fechamento.reprovado:
The last round ends late. Your name finished in the lower half of the table, and you learn what everyone learns in their first final: here, every game is a final.

On the train home, Misha says only: "Next year it's in Riga. We play better at home."
dlg.tal_1957.inicio: Moscow! Did you see the audience? I've never played for so many people. In Tbilisi I nearly didn't make it, and look where we are now. Our game is in round eighteen.
dlg.tal_1957.op_tbilisi: How did you get through in Tbilisi?
dlg.tal_1957.tbilisi: One win in the first twelve rounds. One! Then something came unstuck, and I made six points in the last seven. Don't ask me what. If I knew, I'd do it again here.
dlg.tal_1957.depois_vitoria: You beat me, here, in Moscow. I have to tell you something: I was going to sacrifice the rook next move. Just as well there wasn't time.
dlg.tal_1957.depois_derrota: Sorry, my friend. Moscow does that to me: everything seems possible. But it was a beautiful game on both sides.
dlg.tal_1957.depois_empate: A draw between the two from Riga. The Palace crowd will argue about this game for a whole year.
dlg.spassky57.inicio: Spassky. We're the same age, aren't we? So nobody here can call either of us a boy. Shall we play our round?
dlg.spassky57.op_amsterda: What was it like beating Smyslov?
dlg.spassky57.amsterda: It was the only game he lost in Amsterdam. I felt calmer afterwards than before, which is strange. I think I found out that they're flesh and blood too.
dlg.spassky57.depois_vitoria: Well played. I didn't see your plan coming. That almost never happens to me.
dlg.spassky57.depois_derrota: Good game. You'll see: we'll cross paths many more times.
dlg.spassky57.depois_empate: A draw. Fair. Twenty against twenty, nobody gave way.
dlg.petrosian57.inicio: Petrosian. So you're the other one from Riga. I'll warn you of something, out of politeness: I don't usually lose. Sit down.
dlg.petrosian57.depois_vitoria: Hm. It's been a long time since anyone caught me like that. I'll study this game very carefully.
dlg.petrosian57.depois_derrota: You attacked too early. Against me, almost everyone attacks too early.
dlg.petrosian57.depois_empate: A draw. I like well-played draws. This was one.
dlg.keres57.inicio: Keres. You're from Riga, aren't you? I've played a lot in your city. Welcome to the final. Here everyone starts from zero, even me.
dlg.keres57.vizinho: He beat me in a clock simul in Riga, a few years ago. I confess I don't remember the game. He, I'm told, remembers every move.
dlg.keres57.depois_vitoria: Congratulations, young man. You played like someone who wasn't afraid of me, and that's why you won.
dlg.keres57.depois_derrota: Good game. Don't lose heart: losing to me is what happens most in this hall.
dlg.keres57.depois_empate: A draw. Correct. I'll tell them in Tallinn that dangerous players are being born in Riga.
dlg.bronstein57.inicio: Bronstein. You're Tal's friend? He plays the way I wanted to play at his age. And you, how do you play? Let's find out.
dlg.bronstein57.op_match: What was the match with Botvinnik like?
dlg.bronstein57.match: Twelve all. Two games to go and I was a point ahead. The rest you read in the papers. Don't think about it today: today the game is here.
dlg.bronstein57.depois_vitoria: What a strange game. I like strange games, even when I lose.
dlg.bronstein57.depois_derrota: You looked for the right move. I looked for the move nobody would look for. Sometimes it works.
dlg.bronstein57.depois_empate: A draw. Everything balanced, like a chemist's scales.
dlg.arbitro_1957.inicio: The final starts at the same hours every day, and the hall fills up long before. The wall boards show every game to the audience. Silence on the stage, please.
dlg.arbitro_1957.op_publico: Is it this crowded every day?
dlg.arbitro_1957.publico: Every day. And outside, in the street, there's another wall board for those who couldn't get in. In Moscow, young man, chess is a show. Play as if nobody were watching.
not.n1956_amsterda.texto: The Candidates tournament has ended in Holland: Vasily Smyslov won with 11½ points and will challenge Botvinnik. Keres was second with 10. Young Boris Spassky, nineteen, was the only one to beat the winner.
not.n1956_olimpiada.texto: Thirty-four countries played the chess Olympiad in Moscow. The USSR won with 31 points, ahead of Yugoslavia and Hungary, but lost a team match at an Olympiad for the first time: to Hungary, in the fourth round.
not.n1956_fischer.texto: In New York, the American Robert Fischer, thirteen, beat master Donald Byrne with Black, with a queen sacrifice on move 17. Over there they call it "the game of the century".
not.n1955_gotemburgo.texto: The Interzonal tournament has ended in Sweden: David Bronstein won with 15 points, ahead of Keres and the Argentine Panno. Nine players qualified for the Candidates tournament.
